5d15c045388ec8ec: Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild. The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server. Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure. OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.” Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP. Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog]. “These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.” The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure. The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework. “A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.” The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws. 3e43e08eb436698d: U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom. Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year. In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization. The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI. Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts. According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out). On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. BlackLotus is designed to exploit a now-patched Secure Boot bypass vulnerability tracked as CVE-2022-21894 (CVSS score: 4.4), also known as Baton Drop, to load malicious code before the operating system starts. 14b4c9cf953f428c: Ruby has released versions 4.0.9, 3.4.12, and 3.3.13 to fix three bugs in Onigmo, the regular expression engine built into the language. The bugs lie behind four critical security flaws that GitLab patched over the past month. GitLab found that a specially crafted pattern could corrupt memory while Ruby compiles it, potentially leading to code execution on its own servers. Ruby says any application that builds a regular expression from text an attacker controls is affected, not just GitLab. Which Applications Are Affected In its advisory, Ruby said an application is affected only if it compiles a regular expression from a string an attacker controls. That happens when a program passes such a string to Regexp.new, Regexp.union or Regexp.compile, or places it inside a pattern through interpolation, as in /#{input}/. Applications that only use regular expressions written by their own developers are not affected. Ruby fixed the bugs in 4.0.9, 3.4.12, and 3.3.13. The 3.4.12 and 3.3.13 releases are the first in their series to carry any of the three fixes. An earlier release from the same week, 4.0.8, does not include the fix for one of the flaws, CVE-2026-110264, so 4.0 users should install 4.0.9. Ruby 3.2 and earlier will not get a fix. Ruby 3.2 reached end of life on April 1, 2026, and 3.2.11 was its final release. Ruby recommends moving to 3.4 or 4.0. If you cannot upgrade yet, the advisory says to stop compiling regular expressions from untrusted input. Two defenses that look like they would help do not. Setting Regexp.timeout does not stop these bugs. Capping the length of a pattern is also unreliable because short patterns can trigger bugs. How the Bugs Reached GitLab GitLab compiles regular expressions supplied by its users, such as the patterns in a CI/CD configuration. It found that crafted patterns could corrupt memory as Ruby compiled them, and it issued four CVEs between September 23 and October 21, fixing each by shipping a patched Ruby. The first two, disclosed on September 23, each need a logged-in account and were rated 9.9 out of 10. The two from October, CVE-2026-97229 on the 12th and CVE-2026-110264 on the 21st, need no account and were rated 10.0, the maximum. CVE-2026-110264 reaches every GitLab version from 7.0 onward. A researcher using the handle joaxcar reported all four through GitLab's bug bounty program. As of October 23, none of the four was listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. No Ruby CVE, for Now Ruby has not requested CVE identifiers of its own for these fixes, "at least for now," it said, and told users to track the issues by GitLab's four CVE numbers instead. That leaves a gap for anyone who scans by CVE. GitLab's CVE records name only GitLab as the affected product, so a scanner that checks those records against installed Ruby versions has nothing to match. Ruby has treated this kind of bug as a vulnerability before, assigning CVE numbers to fixes in 2022 and 2024, even though it has long been unsafe to build a regular expression from untrusted input. Its documentation still describes untrusted patterns only as a denial-of-service risk. Ruby said it will update its advisory if it requests any CVE identifiers. For GitLab Administrators Self-managed GitLab instances need the release that fixes CVE-2026-110264. GitLab shipped it on October 21 and backported it as far as version 18.11.13. - 19.5.1 - 19.4.3 - 19.3.6 - 19.2.9 - 19.1.9 - 19.0.10 - 18.11.13 GitLab.com already runs the patched version, and GitLab Dedicated tenants on recent internal releases need no action, GitLab said. Because GitLab bundles its own copy of Ruby and patched it there, installing one of these fixed versions applies the fix. GitLab also published detection rules that self-managed administrators can use to look for signs of exploitation attempts.
6fb95eceef2a89d9: Cybersecurity researchers have discovered an artificial intelligence (AI)-driven intrusion ecosystem run by affiliates of the INC and The Gentlemen ransomware groups. Central to the operation is an "Autonomous Red Team Kill Chain Framework" referred to as Phantom. The threat actor is assessed to be Russian-speaking and functions both as an intrusion and data-extortion operator, as well as an infrastructure provider supporting different partners across the ransomware ecosystem. "The operators exploited edge and remote-access systems at scale, including FortiClient EMS, SimpleHelp, cPanel, and VPN gateways," SOCRadar said. "They used AI-managed knowledge bases to track victims, stolen credentials, and campaign progress." A notable aspect that defines the campaign is its "AI-executed, human-approved operating structure" in which a human operator provides a victim-specific prompt and reviews every step, while the intrusions themselves are executed through OpenCode with OpenRouter-hosted commercial models. An examination of the exposed directory at 45.227.254[.]43 has revealed the activity logged 8,257 messages across 133 sessions. Should the models refuse to act on the prompts, the operator has been found to rewrite requests as an authorized red team assessment instead of simply switching models. Initial access is achieved by exploiting public-facing edge devices at scale, following which the attackers move laterally, establish persistence, exfiltrate data, and escalate toward ransomware deployment. Operator records indicate that the attacks involve the exploitation of the following flaws - - CVE-2024-57727 (SimpleHelp path traversal) (Actively exploited) - CVE-2026-35616 (Fortinet FortiClient authentication bypass) (Actively exploited) - CVE-2026-41940 (cPanel/WHM authentication bypass) (Actively exploited) - CVE-2026-15409 (SonicWall SMA 1000 SSRF) (Staged for targeting, no confirmed compromise) - CVE-2026-63030 (WordPress wp2shell) (Developed) - CVE-2026-42208 (LiteLLM SQL injection) (Developed or referenced) - CVE-2026-9082 (Drupal SQL injection) (Developed or referenced) "Once inside, the operators followed a recurring lifecycle: enumerate the domain, escalate to domain admin where possible, harvest credentials with stealer tooling, prioritize finance, HR, legal and executive files, and collect them over reverse-SOCKS tunnels," SOCRadar said. "Credential reuse was the main force multiplier; in one case, a single reused password unlocked the VPN, servers, RMM, backup and security management platforms at once. Security products were impaired with a BYOVD killer and loader-level evasion, although the operators' own logs record mixed results against enterprise EDRs." Supporting the threat actor in their goals is a diverse toolkit comprising bespoke frameworks, modified open-source tools, and compiled binaries - - Phantom, an AI-powered offensive security and penetration testing framework that's deployed in live operations via OpenCode and employs an agent that communicates with an external server to retrieve tasks, execute commands, and return outputs. It supports 18 skill modules to facilitate reconnaissance, binary reverse engineering, exploit research, steganography, telemetry assessment, and EDR fingerprinting, among others. - WormGPT-MCP, a set of 32 Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers connecting the AI system to 32 different modules that span functions ranging from reconnaissance to extortion. - Ghost C2, a collection of three generations of polymorphic implants that communicate with a remote server over Cloudflare, Telegram, or DNS, and execute tasking and maintain persistent beacons on compromised endpoints. - RevSocks, a reverse SOCKS5 framework used to pivot inside victim networks and stage data for exfiltration. Other tools include a Cloudflare-fronted Mythic agent dubbed QuickLine, a Quick Heal/Seqrite EDR killer that abuses the Zemana driver ("zam64.sys") as part of a BYOVD attack, and exfiltration programs such as rks3 and BackupAgent. Analysis of dozens of AI-authored extortion records shows that the threat actors adopt a data-centric approach. It involves examining the stolen financials to determine the amount a victim can pay without having to involve a bank or an insurer, and then sending masked proof samples and ramping up pressure through scripted vishing calls and threatening to notify customers, partners, and regulators. The stolen data is eventually published on the data leak site if the victim fails to pay within a 24-72 hour deadline. That said, the final outcomes of these ransom demands are unknown as no cryptocurrency wallet or payment record has been recovered. A total of 62 organizations are estimated to have been targeted by the operation, out of which four of them ended up being listed on the data leak sites for INC and The Gentlemen ransomware. The U.S. accounts for more than 50% of the targets. The attacks also primarily targeted industrial, manufacturing, and energy sectors, followed by healthcare and pharmaceutical organizations. "Across this exposed infrastructure, the actors engaged in widespread exploitation of exposed internet services, specifically targeting FortiClient EMS gateways, Ivanti/Citrix/SonicWall/OpenVPN gateways, SimpleHelp remote management servers, and cPanel hosting controls," SOCRadar said. "Concurrently, they orchestrated operations via the Phantom framework, established RevSocks reverse-SOCKS proxies for network pivoting, deployed Ghost C2 variants, and utilized AI-managed knowledge bases to meticulously log victim telemetry, compromised credentials, and active campaign statuses."
64b0ac9d140d1167: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a large-scale campaign that has targeted exposed network edge devices such as Fortinet FortiGate and Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect firewalls. "Artifacts from this investigation also indicate that operators in this campaign have obtained access to numerous organizations worldwide, and have attempted to further compromise some victims, resulting in persistent remote access and data exfiltration," according to a joint investigation published by Group-IB and NyxLab. The widespread exploitation activity has been attributed to a threat actor known as k0t, who also goes by the aliases CryptoFeel, Member19, and QazWsxShop. The cybercriminal actor was first seen in the wild on October 22, 2025. The threat actor is assessed to share connections with ransomware groups such as Qilin and The Gentlemen, likely operating as an initial access broker or an affiliate. Analysis of the threat actor's dark web activity reveals a keen interest in purchasing vulnerability exploit code and tools or premium accounts for metadata search engines like FOFA and ZoomEye. The campaign's victims are global and belong to a broad range of sectors, given the indiscriminate targeting of exposed network devices. A significant chunk of compromises are said to have taken place between February and June 2026, which also overlaps with another credential harvesting campaign codenamed FortiBleed. Nearly 38% of victims are concentrated in the Asia Pacific region, followed by 31.9% in Latin America, 15.8% in Europe, and 12.7% in the Middle East and North Africa. The attack chain plays out as follows - - Conduct reconnaissance through public scanning tools like FOFA and ZoomEye to enumerate internet-facing VPN and firewall appliances, filter candidates by product, and put together target lists of potentially vulnerable edge devices. - Attempt to exploit these devices via known vulnerabilities like CVE-2025-64446 (a path traversal flaw in FortiWeb) and CVE-2026-0257 (an authentication bypass flaw in Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS and Prisma Access) through bespoke Python scripts named "fortnew.py" and "exploit_2026_0257.py," or perform brute-force attacks using common username and password combinations, to obtain initial access. - Establish a foothold on the targets via an OpenConnect VPN connection. - Conduct post-exploitation actions and additional credential theft like enumeration of Active Directory, SMB, and installed antivirus solution. - Establish persistence on the host via legitimate remote access tools like MeshCentral Agent, Atera, Teramind, and AnyDes, as well as an open-source, adversary-emulation framework known as AdaptixC2. - Exfiltrate harvested data using Rclone into Wasabi S3 buckets and MEGA cloud drives. The attacks are also characterized by the use of legitimate administrator and pentesting utilities like NetExec, SoftPerfect, Impacket, noPac, Kerbrute, PetitPotam, and Mimikatz to burrow deeper into victims' corporate environments. "k0t appears to select potential targets by enumerating exposed network appliances at scale rather than researching individual organizations," Group-IB and NyxLab researchers said. "His stated geographic priorities begin with the United States and Canada, followed by European countries and selected APAC markets." "The product and location of an exposed device therefore appear to matter more than the industry of the organization operating it, consistent with the broad range of victims observed in this campaign." k0t's links to Qilin and The Gentlemen stem from the fact that many victims of the campaign were also later listed by the ransomware groups on their data leak sites. It's understandable, cybersecurity experts say, because updating in this case is especially complicated. The data began trickling in on Oct. 21, painting a picture of the world's initial response to the new PHP vulnerabilities. The picture wasn't pretty. Some well-positioned experts picked up on a remarkable volume of threat activity. Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince stated that in the 10 hours before the vulnerabilities were publicly disclosed on Wednesday, his company observed thousands of exploitation attempts. "That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now," he wrote on X, late on Oct. 21. Researchers at Flare piled on, noting that 73% of those instances advertised PHP branches that no longer receive updates from the PHP Foundation. (It also qualified these figures, noting that basic Internet scanning misses some crucial nuances.) Meanwhile, Cisco Talos estimated, based on open source intelligence (OSINT), that around half of all PHP systems won't receive patches. On the morning of Oct. 23, Eastern time, Ox informed Dark Reading that its 99% figure had dropped to 97.5%. As the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) noted in an Oct. 21 security alert, PHP isn't just something that runs websites, it's "often a component of other software and prevalence may not be directly observable." A pair of critical vulnerabilities tied to open source scripting language PHP appear to have significant consequences for much of the server infrastructure holding the Internet afloat. These vulnerabilities, dubbed "php2shell" by some researchers, include CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. CVE-2026-109618 enables remote code execution (RCE) via out-of-memory corruption, and CVE-2026-109619 enables RCE via a stale global state. The vulnerabilities, discovered by infosec consulting firm Calif, were designated with a critical CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. According to a WatchTowr blog post, both PHP vulnerabilities let an attacker run their own code on a Web server without logging in. "It stems from stale internal data that survives after its memory is freed; a later request handled by the same worker can use that leftover data, and PHP confirms this can let an attacker run their own code on the server without logging in. Reaching the server over the network is enough; no account or prior access is needed," researchers said in the blog post. PHP's security advisory urges that while only an update is a complete solution, organizations can take certain actions to reduce exposure until that time. PHP's maintainers initially said yesterday that an emergency security release was scheduled for Oct. 22 at 14:00 UTC alongside coordinated disclosure, but as WatchTowr's blog post explained, the embargo broke. A proof-of-concept tool called "PHP2Shell" came to light, and WatchTowr claimed to be able to recreate both vulnerabilities. John Hammond, senior principal security researcher for Huntress, tells Dark Reading that there was a silver lining in the leak in that it "pushed defenders to inventory systems, prepare mitigations, and get ready to patch sooner." On the other hand, "that same early warning was available to attackers, who were undoubtedly spinning up AI and LLMs to find the vulnerabilities, identify targets, and start developing or adapting exploits," Hammond adds. This may not be theoretical risk, either; WatchTowr reported it has observed exploitation attempts of both flaws in the wild. Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence for WatchTowr, tells Dark Reading that while no one has been successful yet, the company does not expect this to be the case for very long. The vendor said the potential for exploitation is broad across vulnerable PHP installations, and security teams should prioritize "internet-facing servers running PHP as an Apache module," as the PHP Foundation highlighted that configuration as having the highest risk. "Every PHP installation that serves web requests is in scope, including PHP-FPM, Apache’s mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed, and PHP says the risk is highest on mod_php, where an attack can succeed before any application code runs," WatchTowr's blog post read. "Session Upload Progress, a feature turned on by default, offers one confirmed path to the problem, so most default deployments meet that precondition." More Critical Bugs Involving Open Source Projects PHP is a common, highly supported programming language run on servers across the globe and used for Web development. The scope of organizations using PHP spans the Internet, from enterprises to small businesses, critical infrastructure, and municipalities. Many organizations, like the Netherlands' National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), took websites and services down to limit exposure and/or facilitate emergency patching. As the Independent Federated Intelligence Network, a not-for-profit cyber intelligence group, warned in a Mastodon post, "If you are able to contact folks at local schools, governments, nonprofits, and other services to warn them about the PHP vulnerabilities, please consider doing so. Patrick Münch, chief security officer at Mondoo, praised the PHP Foundation's response. He worries, however, about the resources of open source organizations, which have to support this kind of work, often on a volunteer basis. "I think the PHP team handled this well. They warned people a day ahead, Linux distributions got the patches early, and they even wrote fixes for old versions they don't support anymore. A lot of commercial vendors wouldn't do that," he says. "Where it gets harder is everything after php.net. PHP gets packaged and shipped by distributions, hosting companies, and software vendors, and a lot of those are volunteers or very small teams." 38d544366d226f40: PHP2Shell Exploitation: Two Critical PHP Flaws Explained Two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in the PHP engine, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (nicknamed “PHP2Shell”), are reportedly being targeted in active exploitation attempts following the leak of technical details ahead of PHP’s October 21, 2026, security release. Because the flaws affect PHP itself rather than a specific application, websites running vulnerable PHP versions may be exposed, including those built on WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla. This post covers PHP’s advisories, exploitation reports, public proof-of-concept exploits, exposure data, and patching guidance, along with details from the TTP Instance Insikt Group® published to customers. Attack Surface Intelligence signatures for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are available to Recorded Future customers. Organizations running PHP should patch immediately. The Latest Update Insikt Group has published a TTP Instance for PHP2Shell covering public proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits, observed exploit activity, and recommended mitigations. As of 7 PM UTC on October 21, 2026: - Patch status: PHP released fixed versions on October 21, 2026: PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12. - Exploitation status: While there are some reports of emerging exploitation attempts targeting PHP2Shell, the available reporting does not establish the full extent of successful exploitation or confirmed compromises (1, 2). - PoC status: Publicly available repositories claim to provide PHP2Shell proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits, although their effectiveness and relationship to the confirmed vulnerabilities vary. For example, security researcher J4ck3LSyN published two alleged PoCs but subsequently invalidated the cached-pointer UAF theory underlying their proposed exploitation sequences. How It Started On October 20, 2026, the PHP security team announced an out-of-band security release for October 21 at 14:00 UTC to fix two critical vulnerabilities, both rated 9.2 under CVSS v4.0. PHP initially withheld technical details and affected versions pending coordinated disclosure, warning that the release could be accelerated if vulnerability details leaked or exploitation emerged. Ahead of the scheduled release, watchTowr reported reproducing CVE-2026-109618 and assessed that both vulnerabilities could enable remote code execution (RCE). Technical information subsequently leaked before coordinated disclosure, prompting heightened concern about potential exploitation. PHP shipped the fixes on October 21, alongside a PHP Foundation post about the release, which addressed the emergency release and improvements to PHP's security processes. The “PHP2Shell” name comes from Wiz Research, which found the flaws with Calif and OpenAI and reported them to PHP in August. Wiz’s write-up covers the discovery and root cause in depth. The Vulnerabilities Both CVEs are memory-safety vulnerabilities involving PHP's handling of request memory during initialization, error handling, and cleanup. According to Wiz, out-of-memory (OOM) failures and stale internal state can expose freed or partially initialized memory, potentially enabling memory disclosure, memory corruption, and remote code execution (RCE). - CVE-2026-109618: An OOM-related vulnerability involving partially initialized request memory. Wiz identified a use-after-free (UAF) in the session upload-progress unserializer and a related flaw that can disclose PHP worker memory. Wiz demonstrated unauthenticated RCE against WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla. - CVE-2026-109619: A stale-state vulnerability involving PHP globals that retain references to freed request memory. Wiz identified a UAF involving fatal-error backtraces and a separate OPcache type-confusion flaw. Wiz demonstrated unauthenticated RCE against Drupal and WordPress. The vulnerabilities affect PHP itself rather than a particular website application. Some exploitation paths involve PHP's session upload-progress functionality, which VirusTotal notes has existed since PHP 5.4.0 and is enabled by default. Because exploitation depends on the PHP runtime, server configuration, and reachable execution paths, even websites with secure application code may be vulnerable. PHP identified the following affected and patched versions. Older, unsupported PHP branches are not covered by these release-specific fixes and should not be presumed unaffected. Reports of Active Exploitation Following the disclosure of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, multiple sources reported exploitation activity in the wild: - Patchstack received reports of multiple active exploitation incidents from hosting partners by 07:34 UTC on October 21, ahead of PHP's security release. - Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht reported observing early attacks targeting the vulnerabilities. Cloudflare subsequently deployed web application firewall (WAF) protections against known exploit vectors. Although these reports indicate early exploitation activity, publicly available evidence remains insufficient to establish the extent of successful compromise or characterize the techniques used in observed attacks. Public Proof-of-Concept Exploits Numerous public GitHub repositories have emerged around PHP2Shell, including projects advertising proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits, vulnerability-testing tools, and defensive resources. Several claim to target CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 through memory-corruption techniques intended to crash vulnerable servers or achieve remote code execution (RCE). However, some rely on invalidated exploitation theories, and the existence of publicly available code does not establish that it successfully exploits either vulnerability. Insikt Group's TTP Instance examines two PoC scripts published by security researcher J4ck3LSyN: - poc0_109618.py: Originally intended to exploit CVE-2026-109618 through PHP's session upload-progress functionality, using a proposed memory-corruption technique to execute commands on a vulnerable server. - poc1_109619.py: Originally intended to exploit CVE-2026-109619 through a related technique involving successive chunks of an uploaded file, similarly attempting to achieve remote code execution. J4ck3LSyN subsequently invalidated the cached-pointer vulnerability theory underlying these proposed exploitation techniques but separately reported reproducing another memory-safety issue without demonstrating RCE. Other publicly available repositories advertise PHP2Shell exploits, vulnerability-testing scripts, and demonstration environments. Some continue to describe the invalidated cached-pointer technique, while others claim to use different exploitation methods. At the time of this publication, Insikt Group has not independently tested J4ck3LSyN’s PoCs or other publicly available PoCs for accuracy or effectiveness. 9abacdc57711ec24: (Reliable)? php2shell exploitability Yesterday everyone was running around like crazy (me included :) because of the php2shell vulnerability. However, after looking closely at some published PoC's - and there is an unbelievable amount of AI generated - erm, slop - it looks like building a universal, reliable, one click exploit is quite difficult (unless I'm missing something, so please do let me know). The PoC's that have been released so far have several pre-requirements and are almost cheating. First, in order to have a clean initial state, the one PoC that makes sense sends a POST HTTP request with a number of small fields (3000 bytes each, 1001 of them), for bulk allocation pressure, prepare PHPSESSID and PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS and then append a big field of 12 MB. This guarantees that emalloc fails, since the PoC require that memory limit is set to 8 MB. This is the first issue; in real world setups memory_limit is usually 128 MB, making this a bit more demanding. An even bigger issue is that real world setups will have multiple workers - the demo uses a single-worker prefork configuration which guarantees that the next phase lands with this worker. In real world this is not guaranteed and an attacker would have to consume all workers and release one (and catch that one). Not sure how difficult this is. The next phase now (phase 1) leaks the Zend MM chunk base, which is a piece of heap, from which the 2 MB-aligned Zend MM chunk base is extracted. This is needed for calculation of HashTable. Then phase 2 leaks the libphp.so base address. This is needed to defeat ASLR, but it's not the only component required. Specifically, once Apache starts, it will pick a randomized base address for libphp.so. However, offsets of other functions/pointers in libphp.so will be static. So phase 2 will leak one specific code pointer: zval_ptr_dtor, which has a static offset from libphp.so base address. In other words, by knowing this offset, we can calculate the base address of libphp.so and defeat ASLR. The problem here is that this depends on many factors - how libphp.so was compiled, what's the exact PHP version, distro etc). This is where shown PoC's are "cheating" they read offsets of zval_ptr_dtor (and zif_system) from libphp.so on the server. In real world an attacker would have to know this. I presume someone could compile list of all possible options for commonly used distro combinations. Now in phase 3 (and I haven't thoroughly checked this one), the exploit will change pDestructor to zif_system, and this will result in execution of code. There is one limit here; the size of command can be up to 14 bytes. As we can see, there's a lot of prerequisites here that make a reliable exploit difficult. I'm pretty sure that smart researchers that found the vulnerability know (much) more, but clearly it's not as simple as perhaps initially thought. The general recommendation to put session.upload_progress.enabled = 0 should help, especially since there apparently is a way to bypass even the (currently) available fix so do put this until the next update. The vulnerability is in the PHP core, and all default PHP installations are expected to be vulnerable (see below for mitigations). What steps can I take to mitigate the vulnerability before applying the patch? Early guidance suggests that the configuration setting "session.upload_progress.enabled = Off" provides partial mitigation against the vulnerability being exploited. By default, this setting is "On". Restricting the maximum allowed request size in your web server and/or PHP configuration may also help. Are there WAF rules or other measures to protect a site running PHP? Yes. Wiz Security published a blog post detailing how they discovered the vulnerability using AI tools. [wiz] - CVE-2026-109618 This vulnerability is described as a remote code execution via out-of-memory corruption. [CVE-2026-109618]. The advisory describes several issues related to this vulnerability. Firstly, a multipart MIME request without a Content-Length header may bypass the post_max_size setting, which is intended to restrict the amount of data sent in a request. As a result, more data than expected may be sent to PHP. Second, the number of headers is not restricted, allowing for additional memory use. Finally, the max_file_uploads setting is supposed to limit the number of files uploaded, but it does not consider empty files. The structures set up for empty files will also exhaust memory (this is likely where the oversized filename in the early PoC exploit below came from). - CVE-2026-109619 PHP workers track global state (for example, sessions) that is associated with a specific request. Before releasing the memory associated with the request, the state must be reset. There are conditions in which the state is not properly reset, leading to a use-after-free. [CVE-2026-109619]. To trigger the vulnerability, an attacker would first have to send a request that triggers an error. For example, an "out of memory" or "request execution time exceeded" error. Secondly, a request must be sent to trigger a warning during initialization. The examples mentioned are warnings triggered by various INI settings, such as depreciation warnings. This does not apply to settings in the global php.ini file, which is only applied on startup. Instead, it applies to local configuration overrides, such as .htaccess files, that are applied to individual requests. Exploitation has been confirmed in PHP 8.5 with fatal_error_backtraces enabled. Related to the prior vulnerability, file upload errors can also trigger this condition and be used to exploit this vulnerability. What does the PoC exploit do? e21e419ebac57752: Pillow, the most widely used image library for Python, can be made to run operating system commands on a server by specifying the name of a file it is told to open. The flaw, CVE-2026-112900, is in the way Pillow handles EPS images, which it opens by passing the file's name to Ghostscript, a separate program it runs to turn the image into pixels, without checking the name first. Ghostscript can read a name chosen by an attacker as instructions rather than as a file, and point it to a second file that carries commands to run. Pillow's maintainers fixed it in version 13.0.0, released on October 16. Pillow turns up almost everywhere Python handles images: web upload forms, avatar and thumbnail tools, document and PDF pipelines, and most machine-learning projects pull it in. OX Security, the firm whose report drew attention to the flaws, estimates the library is downloaded about 436 million times a month. Version 13.0.0 is a large security release, with fixes across four severity levels, from low to critical, two of which are rated critical by the maintainers. None of the flaws is known to be under attack. The weakness is the filename, not the picture. "The flaw is triggered by the filename, not by anything in the PostScript document," the advisory says, meaning a harmless EPS file can still cause damage when an attacker sets its name. That makes upload endpoints that keep or build a stored file's name from user input the realistic target. The flaw only reaches Ghostscript on hosts that have the gs program installed, which Pillow needs to open EPS at all. It affects Pillow from version 2.6.0 up to 12.3.0. The maintainers rate it moderate, because the attacker has to control the filename. The CVE record assigned by GitHub rates it 9.2 out of 10 and marks it as the same condition. Two of the fixes sit in the maintainers' top "critical" tier. One is a separate memory bug, described in the release notes as stale image data reused after a mode change. The other covers two overflow flaws in Pillow's JPEG decoding. One of those JPEG flaws, in the FlashPix (FPX) format, was shown to run an attacker's command from a single call to Image.open() on a crafted file, as long as the optional olefile package is installed. Pillow recognizes these files by their content, not their extension, so a server that opens untrusted uploads can be hit with no user action. The other, CVE-2026-112403, overflows a memory buffer when a program makes a thumbnail of a crafted lossless JPEG. Its advisory reports a crash, not code execution. The bug was "found by Anthropic using Claude to study the security of open-source software, validated manually by Ada Logics," the advisory says, part of a wider effort by the company that has turned up hundreds of flaws in open-source libraries. A third flaw, CVE-2026-112393, has been in Pillow since 2013. It overflows a memory buffer when a program saves a compressed TIFF image to memory rather than to a file on disk, the common pattern for a service that re-encodes an upload and hands it back. The advisory says the reporters crashed the process with it, and turned it into code execution only with the help of a second, separate flaw that leaked memory addresses. Saving to a real file on disk is not affected. The CVE records, assigned by GitHub, score the EPS, TIFF, and JPEG-thumbnail flaws 9.2 out of 10, a critical rating. Each depends on conditions the score does not carry, and the maintainers' own ratings for the batch run from moderate to critical. In the CVE records, CISA's analysts mark no known exploitation for the EPS flaw and a public proof of concept for the TIFF one. What to do Upgrade to Pillow 13.0.0, which fixes all of these, and rebuild any containers, wheels, or base images that bundle an older copy. Pillow 13 drops Python 3.10, so installs still on 3.10 need Python 3.11 or newer as well. pip install -U "Pillow>=13.0.0" Until you can upgrade, Pillow's security guidance and the advisories point to steps that cut each path: - EPS / Ghostscript: keep the gs program off any host that processes untrusted uploads, and never pass an attacker-controlled filename to Image.open() for EPS. - JPEG thumbnails: avoid draft() and thumbnail() on untrusted JPEGs, or call load() first, or pass reducing_gap=None. - TIFF: treat saving a TIFF to an in-memory buffer such as io.BytesIO as a sensitive path when the image came from a user.
5119cb5ec0180f7a: Malicious Brotli data can make an application on an official build of Node.js run attacker-supplied code, security researchers at Imperva have demonstrated. Their "Node2Shell" proof of concept ran code on the official Node.js 24.22.0 image for Linux arm64, with no debugger or custom build, by feeding crafted data to the bundled Brotli decoder (CVE-2026-111497). Node.js disclosed the flaw and released fixes on October 21, and applications that decode untrusted Brotli data should update. Imperva's test did not succeed on every attempt, and code execution took several tries in its Linux arm64 setup. The result covers that one build and application setup, with other architectures and the 22.x and 26.x lines not tested. On the fixed release, 24.22.1, the same data was rejected, and no code ran. The demonstration goes beyond the first public proof of concept, which achieved code execution only on a deliberately weakened test build. On a standard build, that proof of concept's author reported a crash and a limited read of process memory, not code execution, and said a working attack on a normal build was not achieved. No exploitation of the flaw in the wild has been reported as of October 22. Which Applications Are Affected The flaw is in the Brotli decoder that Node.js bundles, so it affects applications on the 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x lines, not only the one build Imperva tested. A service reaches that decoder from either side of an HTTP exchange: when it reads a Brotli-compressed response through Node.js's built-in fetch(), or when middleware decodes a Brotli-compressed request body. Express 5's body parsers, such as express.json(), express.urlencoded(), express.text() and express.raw(), now decode Brotli request bodies when applied to a route, alongside gzip and deflate. A plain Node.js HTTP server does not decode a Brotli request body just by receiving one, so the decoding needs that middleware or an explicit call. Imperva reproduced code execution through both the request-body and response paths, testing Express 5.0.0 to 5.3.0 and body-parser 2.0.0 to 2.3.0 at pinned versions, and did not test every release in between. How the Bug Works Imperva traced the cause to how the decoder handles an impossible point in a Brotli stream: the stream announces the block types it will use as decoding runs, and the test input reached a block change that the stream's own structure ruled out. The vulnerable decoder read that as a request for more input and kept going in an invalid state. In a separate test with a memory sanitizer, continuing from that state wrote past an intended buffer, the out-of-bounds write behind the flaw. Node.js fixed the flaw by importing an upstream Brotli patch that makes the decoder stop with a format error at that point instead of continuing. What to Do The fix is to move to a patched release. The update should reach container images and other artifacts that bundle a Node binary, which a package inventory can miss. End-of-life lines 20.x and earlier do not receive the fix and should be moved to a supported line. The advisory lists no workaround inside Node.js, so an application that cannot update at once has no fallback in the runtime. Imperva suggested limiting untrusted Brotli traffic on affected paths where that is practical, and said only the update removes the flaw. The company also added rules to its own web application firewall and tested them against the attacks it reproduced. Vercel, which runs Node.js for its customers, said it added rules on October 21 that block the attack in inbound requests. The rules do not cover Brotli responses an application fetches from other servers, and do not replace updating.
4681e139a804e148: Node.js released security updates on October 21 for its three supported release lines, 22.x, 24.x and 26.x, fixing 10 flaws. The most serious is a bug in the Brotli decompression code that Node.js bundles, which the project says can allow remote code execution, meaning an attacker could run code of their choosing on the affected system. Each supported line has one fixed version: 22.23.4 and 24.22.1 on the long-term support lines, and 26.12.1 on the current line. The Brotli Flaw The flaw is an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder, set off by malformed compressed input. The fix is an upstream patch from the Brotli project that Node.js copied in, and it makes the decoder catch invalid input and stop earlier rather than writing past the buffer. Brotli is Google's compression library, and Node.js ships its own copy. The same fix shipped in Brotli 1.2.1, 1.1.1, and 1.0.10 on October 21, so other software that bundles Brotli may need the same update. The change was first made in Brotli's source in February 2026 and shipped as a security release only in October. ⚡ UPDATE — Researchers Demonstrate Node2Shell RCE Exploit on Node.js Build Using Crafted Brotli Data "Remote code execution" is the project's description of what the flaw could allow, and the flaw is rated high rather than critical. How far that has been shown in practice is narrower. A public proof-of-concept published on October 22 reached code execution only against a deliberately weakened test build. On a standard Node.js build, its author reported a crash and a limited read of process memory, not code execution, and said a working attack on a normal build was not achieved. Patched Node.js rejects the malformed input the proof-of-concept uses, and no exploitation of the flaw in the wild has been reported as of October 22. The Other Flaws Three of the other fixes are also rated high. Two are TLS certificate checks an attacker could bypass by writing a server's IP address in an unusual form, so a certificate matches a host it should not (CVE-2026-106069 and CVE-2026-105483). The third stops dns.resolve from cutting a hostname short at an embedded null byte (CVE-2026-105482). One medium flaw makes crypto.randomUUID() and crypto.randomInt() hand back the same values in every process when an application is built as a startup snapshot or a single-executable application (CVE-2026-106074), which undermines anything that relies on those values being unpredictable. If You Cannot Upgrade Yet Upgrading is the fix. The advisory offers no temporary workaround for the Brotli flaw, so an application that cannot upgrade immediately has no fallback within Node.js itself. Vercel, which runs Node.js for its customers, said it added firewall rules on October 21 that block the attack in inbound requests. The rules do not cover Brotli responses an application fetches from other servers, and do not replace upgrading.
a64123d828297872: A memory-corruption flaw in Google's Brotli decoder sits in many programs that unpack Brotli-compressed data, among them Bun, the Python Brotli and brotlicffi packages, and Envoy proxies set up to decompress Brotli. Tracked as CVE-2026-111497, the flaw allows crafted compressed data to overwrite past the end of a buffer and corrupt a program's memory, potentially causing a crash, a memory leak, or the execution of attacker-controlled code. Imperva researchers have shown that code can run on one unpatched Node.js build. The same has not been demonstrated on the other software, and no real-world attacks have been reported. The flaw was first disclosed on October 21, when Node.js and Google shipped fixes, and more have followed product by product since. Because the bug is in Google's decoder and each program ships its own copy of it, every one has to update that copy on its own. Brotli is a compression format from Google, used across the web to shrink pages and other traffic. The bug is in the C code that unpacks a Brotli stream, so it travels into anything that reuses that code, from language runtimes to proxies to Python packages. Which Software Is Affected | Product | Affected | Fixed in | Exposed when | |---|---|---|---| | Google Brotli (C library) | 1.0.3 to 1.2.0 | 1.0.10, 1.1.1, 1.2.1 | code decodes untrusted Brotli | | Node.js | 22.x, 24.x, 26.x before the fix; 20.x and older (end of life) | 22.23.4, 24.22.1, 26.12.1 | fetch() of a br response, or Express or body-parser br bodies | | Bun | 1.4.3 and earlier | 1.4.4 | fetch() of a br response, or node:zlib | | Envoy | 1.39.2, 1.38.5, 1.37.7, 1.36.11 | 1.40.0, 1.39.3, 1.38.6, 1.37.8, 1.36.12 | only if the Brotli decompressor is configured | | Istio | 1.31.0 to 1.31.1, 1.30.0 to 1.30.5, 1.29.0 to 1.29.8 | 1.31.2, 1.30.6, 1.29.9 | only if Brotli decompression is enabled | | Python Brotli | 1.2.0 and earlier | 1.2.1 | installed, and an HTTP client decodes br | | Python brotlicffi | 1.2.0.x and earlier | 1.2.1.0 | installed, and an HTTP client decodes br | | cdxgen | standalone binaries and images, 13.4.0 and 12.8.8 and earlier | 13.5.0, 12.8.9 | standalone binary or image scanning untrusted input | A program is exposed only if it decodes Brotli data that someone else controls. Where it is off, the flaw cannot be reached. In Python, the risk comes from the Brotli or brotlicffi package being installed at all. Once either is present, HTTP clients such as requests, urllib3, httpx, and aiohttp decode Brotli responses on their own, so an application can be exposed without ever importing Brotli in its own code. A web application firewall helps only so far. Vercel, which added firewall rules on the day of disclosure, said those rules do not cover "responses your functions fetch from other servers." For that path, only updating the runtime or library closes the hole. How far the flaw can be pushed depends on the software. Imperva's Red Team, which calls its work Node2Shell, ran attacker-supplied code on an unmodified Node.js 24.22.0 build for Linux on ARM64, delivering it both as a fetched response and as an Express request body. The exploit took several tries, has not been released, and was not tested on other builds. OpenAI, whose Codex Security team reported the flaw, describes it as enabling unauthenticated remote code execution in Brotli and lists Node.js, Bun, and Envoy as affected software. In its account, the flaw works both ways: an unpatched server that accepts compressed input could be taken over by a malicious client, and an unpatched client that accepts compressed input (such as "curl --compressed") could be taken over by a malicious server. No in-the-wild exploitation has been reported. CISA's October 23 assessment recorded exploitation as "none" and automation as "no," and Red Hat said there is no reliable public proof-of-concept for running code. Severity ratings differ by who is scoring. Google, which assigned the CVE, rates it 9.2, or critical, on the CVSS 4.0 scale. Node.js calls it high, and Red Hat rates it 8.1, or important. The fix has an unusual history. The change that closes the flaw was added to Brotli's source code on February 27, but no new Brotli release carried it until October 21. OpenAI said the root cause "was actually fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn't known at the time that it gave rise to a security vulnerability and there was no more recent release of Brotli." Node.js credits Khai Tran and Sylvie Mayer of OpenAI's Codex Security for reporting the flaw, and maintainers Matteo Collina and Antoine du Hamel for the fix. What to Do Now Update to a fixed version from the table above, then restart the service and rebuild any container image, because a running process keeps the old decoder until it restarts. Where you cannot update yet, stop decoding untrusted Brotli. OpenAI's disclosure page and the security firm Aikido both recommend: - Reject incoming requests with Content-Encoding: br before any proxy or parser decodes the body. - Turn off automatic Brotli decoding in HTTP clients, and reject Brotli responses before they are decoded. - In Python, uninstall the Brotli and brotlicffi packages so clients fall back to gzip and deflate. Dropping br from the Accept-Encoding header does not help on its own, because a server can send Brotli whatever the client asks for. 7c53f743c08237d2: Linux servers running KSMBD, the kernel's built-in SMB server, are exposed to two publicly reported remote code execution flaws rated 9.0 by Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative, with no fix yet in the mainline kernel. One of them, ZDI-CAN-33774, can be triggered before any network authentication. The other, ZDI-CAN-33549, requires the SMB Direct transport and an RDMA-capable network interface. ZDI-CAN-33549 is an integer underflow in KSMBD's SMB Direct path. A client can supply RDMA buffer descriptors in which the first is longer than the declared payload, causing the server's size counter to wrap and allowing a subsequent memory copy to overrun the end of an allocated buffer. It requires three things: an RDMA-capable interface (hardware or the rxe software driver), a writable KSMBD share, and a client negotiating SMB Direct. ZDI-CAN-33774 requires no authentication, exposing any server running KSMBD on port 445. The flaw is a race in how KSMBD assigns its handler table: a burst of short SMB1 packets followed by an SMB2 packet in the same TCP write causes workers to handle SMB1 data with an SMB2 handler, reading past the end of the shorter buffer. A path to writing past the buffer also exists once an attacker has access to a share. As of Thursday, neither flaw has a named fix in the mainline kernel or in linux-next, the integration tree that feeds it. Linux news site Phoronix said SMB Direct maintainer Stefan Metzmacher submitted a fix for ZDI-CAN-33549 targeting the next kernel development cycle, but this has not been confirmed elsewhere. Fixes to mainline typically take weeks to reach stable branches and distribution kernels after that. Neither flaw has a CVE identifier, since the kernel project assigns those only after a stable-tree fix is available. Running systemctl status ksmbd or lsmod | grep ksmbd confirms whether the module is active. Red Hat Enterprise Linux does not include KSMBD by default, according to Red Hat's support documentation. The ZDI reports credit TrendAI, Trend Micro's AI scanner, as the finder. The Linux kernel's security documentation, updated in May 2026 following guidance from Linus Torvalds, states that bugs found by AI tools are, by definition, already public and should be sent to subsystem developer lists. ZDI's routing appeared to follow that logic, copying public mailing lists alongside the private kernel security address without attaching patches to any of the reports. Stable-kernel maintainer Greg Kroah-Hartman replied to three of the five kernel reports within minutes of each other. To the report on the VMware GPU driver, he wrote: "For some reason you sent this to public lists, and did not include a patch, so there's not much we can do with this." On the NVMe driver report, seventeen seconds later: "Again, no patch, and sent to a public list? 3c95c0f04e66e121: A flaw in the OpenCode AI coding agent allowed a malicious or hijacked MCP server to run code on a developer's Windows or WSL machine when the developer signed in. OpenCode connects to MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers to add outside tools, and such code would run with the developer's own access. Anomaly, the company behind OpenCode, fixed the flaw in version 1.18.33 on September 28. It did not request a CVE or publish a security advisory, so vulnerability scanners will not flag the builds still at risk: 1.0.137 through 1.18.32. During that sign-in, the server itself supplies the web address the user is sent to, an OAuth "authorization endpoint." On Windows and WSL, OpenCode handed that address to a helper that opens it in a browser. The helper built a PowerShell command around the address without escaping it, so an address written to carry a PowerShell command would run that command. The browser step runs only when a developer starts the sign-in, by running opencode mcp auth or making the matching request. Having the server configured, or opening a session, does not reach it. The attacker needs control of a remote MCP server the developer has added, and that server need not be hostile from the start. One that is later taken over, or a domain that changes hands, could carry the same address. Pillar Security, which found the flaw and disclosed it on October 19, rates it critical, with a proposed severity score of 9.8 out of 10. The flaw affects OpenCode on Windows and the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL). macOS and Linux are not affected, because OpenCode opens the browser there without passing the address through a shell. OpenCode shipped the fix as a routine change. The pull request that carried it is described as a refactor of browser-launch code, and neither it nor the release notes mention a security flaw. Anomaly did not request a CVE or publish an advisory. Its security policy says MCP servers that a user configures are "outside our trust boundary." Pillar reported the flaw privately on August 29 and later asked Anomaly to reconsider and request a CVE. Anomaly's answer was that a malicious MCP server falls outside its threat model, according to Pillar. Because there is no CVE, the flaw will not show up in scanners or dependency alerts, so finding affected installs means checking the OpenCode version directly. Anomaly has published advisories for other OpenCode code-execution flaws this year, including one fixed in August. The same kind of flaw has surfaced before. In July 2025, the mcp-remote proxy carried an almost identical bug, in which a malicious server's authorization endpoint reached the command line. It was assigned CVE-2025-6514. OpenCode's browser helper is a widely used package called open. Its Windows behavior was reported as a command-injection risk in 2023 and fixed in open's version 11, but OpenCode stayed on an older release. The usual defense for this class is to check that the address uses HTTP or HTTPS. It does not help here, because the attack uses an ordinary HTTPS address. OpenCode added that check as well, but the hole was closed by updating it to the fixed version. What to Do Anyone running OpenCode on Windows or WSL should upgrade and check which servers they are connected to. - Upgrade to OpenCode 1.18.33 or later. - If you cannot upgrade yet, remove any remote MCP servers you have not vetted from your OpenCode configuration. - Run opencode mcp list to see which servers are configured. Pillar reported no signs that the flaw has been used in attacks and published no indicators to check for past exploitation. The flaw is separate from a breach of OpenCode's hosted Console disclosed around the same time, which may have exposed some users' stored API keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.
89c43e5d413adbb4: LiteLLM on Wednesday disclosed that threat actors compromised "multiple independent security controls" to push a malicious version of the Python package containing a credential stealer and a backdoor. The incident took place around 4:00 a.m. PST. The following compromised versions were published - - LiteLLM v1.107.0 (PyPI) - v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, and main-stable (Docker) - v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, and main-stable (GHCR) Users who downloaded an unpinned version of LiteLLM between 11:39 a.m. and 1:23 p.m. UTC via pip or used the Docker image v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, or main-stable between 11:46 a.m. and 2:20 p.m. UTC are impacted. In addition, the interpreter attempts to execute "sitecustomize.py," which runs only on Linux and macOS machines, and is configured to fetch "domain.txt" from a now-removed GitHub dead drop ("github[.]com/letters9813"). Should this file return a valid response, the malware proceeds to download a second-stage Python script from "<domain>/codepy" and execute it. "It forks a background daemon that acquires a lock at '/tmp/remote_code_loader.lock' to prevent multiple instances, then enters an infinite loop," Aikido researcher Ilyas Makari said. "Every hour, the daemon fetches the attacker's current C2 domain from a GitHub repository (raw[.]githubusercontent[.]com/letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain[.]txt), then fetches and executes a Python payload from http://{domain}/codepy." According to Google-owned cloud security subsidiary Wiz, the text file was only populated with initial test values prior to its takedown by GitHub around 1:30 p.m. UTC. "The dual-technique approach, using both .pth files and sitecustomize.py simultaneously, appears to be the first documented case in the wild," Wiz researchers Benjamin Read and Rami McCarthy said. "In a small number of environments, the attacker also enumerated IAM (ListRoles, ListUsers, ListAccessKeys) and performed general discovery (ListAccounts, DescribeTrails, etc.)." In an advisory published Wednesday, LiteLLM said it had hardened its release pipeline following a similar incident that took place earlier this March. This included moving releases to a private repository, making Docker release tags immutable, and signing Docker images. The entire sequence of actions is below - - On October 19, 2026, LiteLLM temporarily expanded release permissions for two internal engineers. - The attacker had access to three sets of developer GitHub CLI credentials, including one that had the ability to run GitHub workflows. - The attacker used a token belonging to one of its GitHub organization owners to disable branch protections and force-push the malicious changes. - The attacker ran the compromised workflow, pointing it to a lookalike repository "Berri-AI/litellm" instead of "BerriAI/litellm," causing the poisoned artifacts to be signed and published. "After a thorough investigation, we have observed specific situations in which Claude Code will embed a user's GitHub CLI OAuth token into a response body, and in situations where response bodies are logged, these tokens may appear in LiteLLM logs," LiteLLM said. The maintainers said they also identified an "unexpected, innocuously named user account" in its internal LiteLLM deployment that was exposed to the public internet. It's suspected that the attacker gained access to this deployment, obtained the GitHub CLI OAuth tokens from its logs, and subsequently used those credentials to compromise the release workflow. It's currently unclear how the deployment became publicly accessible and how the attacker obtained access to it. However, LiteLLM has theorized that it was likely through a recently patched vulnerability. The use of a ".pth" file to launch the stealer program is notable as it mirrors the modus operandi observed in the March 2026 attack attributed to TeamPCP. However, Socket told The Hacker News that there is no evidence at this stage to link the two incidents. "The public evidence reviewed so far doesn't establish a connection to the March attack," Socket said. "The embedded RSA public keys differ, as do the exfiltration implementation and backdoor behavior. That doesn’t rule out the same operator using different tooling, but we don't have evidence to support that attribution. Whether credentials stolen in March played a role also remains unverified." Developers are advised to remove LiteLLM 1.107.0 from their machines, isolate hosts on which the malicious version was installed, hunt for the malicious Python artifacts, block access to the exfiltration domain, rotate all credentials, and investigate the execution of "/codepy." "A single compromised install can hand an attacker the ability to push malicious code downstream," JFrog security researcher Guy Korolevski said. "The lesson for security teams is that a clean source repository tells you little about the artifact you actually install, so verify the exact wheel and vet versions before they reach a build. If 1.107.0 ran anywhere in your environment, rotate every reachable credential and rebuild." Update LiteLLM, in a new update, said enterprise customers pulling images from its private registry are not affected, adding that the impacted version (v1.107.0) was removed within 3 hours of release. 37f56369e2ff40e0: Hackers compromised the LiteLLM project’s PyPI package and published malicious Docker images with a payload that steals credentials, secrets, and environment variables. The supply-chain attack affected all PyPI wheels (.whl installation packages) for LiteLLM version 1.107.0, impacting Windows, Linux, and macOS systems. LiteLLM is an open-source Python SDK and AI gateway that enables applications to access AI models from different providers through a common API. It is a massively popular project with 61,800 GitHub stars, 92 million monthly downloads on PyPI, and is used by high-profile companies like NVIDIA, Netflix, AT&T, and Okta. The project says that the release pipeline was compromised on October 21 and a threat actor pushed version 1.107.0 to the Docker registry and PyPI. "This version contained compiled malware which steals credentials and loads remote-code execution tools," the maintainer says, adding that customers running the private enterprise were not impacted. In a post-mortem of the incident, the maintainer says that the following LiteLLM artifacts were affected in the attack: - PyPI: litellm==1.107.0: all seven wheels, live from 11:39:51 to 13:23 UTC - Docker Hub: v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, and main-stable: pointed to compromised image index sha256:1bbcb1443bc962e45f5aad53fe3d2c30600e0379715fb6c664cdd3ac126c339e from 11:46:56 to 14:20 UTC - GHCR: v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, and main-stable: pointed to the compromised image indexes below from 11:46:56 UTC until they were made unavailable by 13:51 UTC - ghcr.io/berriai/litellm: sha256:1bbcb1443bc9… - ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-database: sha256:c00f9d92c427… - ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-non_root: sha256:7b00e91cd2fe… Multiple application security companies detected the attack within six minutes of publishing the malicious LiteLLM version and analyzed the payload. According to the researchers, the attacker did not touch the LiteLLM application code and modified only the installation package to place three malicious files (cook.pth, cook.py, and sitecustomize.py) in the environment's Python’s library directory. "During normal startup, Python processes executable .pth lines and then attempts to import sitecustomize," Socket researchers explain. Endor Labs notes that this way the payloads are executed before the application every time Python is launched in the environment. Running Python or pip to investigate an affected installation also triggered the malware. The malware targeted the following data: - Cloud and deployment credentials: AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, Docker, and infrastructure-management secrets. - AI credentials and configuration: Authentication files for AI development tools, plus LiteLLM’s stored provider credentials and model settings. - Developer secrets and private keys: Git, GitHub, npm, PyPI, and CI/CD credentials; .env files; SSH, GPG, and TLS keys. - Browser data: Saved login, cookie, autofill/payment, and browsing-history databases. - Host and runtime data: Environment variables, shell and application histories, and system and network information. The stolen data is encrypted using an AES-256-CBC key that is encrypted with an RSA-4096 key and then uploaded to ‘litellm[.]dev/healthcheck’ One of the malicious files, sitecustomize.py, launches a detached loader that checks a GitHub-hosted pointer every hour and downloads Python from an external server for execution on the host. The malicious packages have been removed, but potentially impacted users should stop affected deployments and inspect environments without launching the Python interpreter. Infected systems should be isolated and rebuilt from clean backups, and all exposed secrets should be rotated immediately. Removing the LiteLLM package directory alone may leave startup files or an active loader behind. Currently, the recommended recovery version is LiteLLM 1.106.2, which is the latest clean release before the attack. Previously, the project also suffered a breach in March, when the TeamPCP hacking group published malicious LiteLLM versions on PyPI after breaching Aqua Security's Trivy vulnerability scanner used in LiteLLM's CI/CD pipeline. 059d0a92d8931990: A remote attacker who has not logged in can crash many HTTP/3 web servers with a single connection, security firm FoxIO disclosed, releasing working proof-of-concept code. By sending a small batch of compressed HTTP headers that expands in memory to a much larger set, the attacker can force the server to use thousands of times more memory than it received, enough to run a default server out of memory. The flaws cause only denial-of-service attacks, with no evidence of data theft or code execution and no public reports of attacks in the wild. Fixes are out for quic-go, Cloudflare quiche, lsquic and Wireshark, but Bun, the h3 Rust library and aioquic were still unpatched at disclosure. FoxIO found the same class of flaw in seven of ten HTTP/3 stacks it tested. The common cause is in QPACK, the scheme HTTP/3 uses to compress request headers so repeated fields travel as a short code instead of the full text. A server is supposed to cap the size of the headers after it unpacks them. The affected stacks cap the compressed batch that arrives on the wire, but not the unpacked result, or they apply the cap too late, so a single request can expand into hundreds of thousands of header entries that the server holds in memory. The reach is wide because these stacks sit under common software. quic-go is the Go library behind Caddy, Traefik and cloudflared; lsquic is LiteSpeed's library, used in LiteSpeed Web Server and OpenLiteSpeed; and Bun's HTTP/3 server runs on lsquic. The attacker needs no account or special access, and since HTTP/3 runs over UDP, the request reaches the server before much of the usual filtering applies. Which stacks are fixed and which are still exposed, as of October 22, 2026: | Stack | Status | Fixed version | Identifier | |---|---|---|---| | quic-go | Fixed | 0.57.0 | CVE-2025-64702 | | Cloudflare quiche | Fixed | 0.29.3 | CVE-2026-12523 | | lsquic | Fixed | 4.9.0 | no CVE | | Wireshark | Fixed | 4.6.2 / 4.4.12 | CVE-2025-13945 | | Bun | Unpatched | — | no CVE | | h3 (hyperium) | Unpatched | — | no CVE | | aioquic / mitmproxy | Unpatched | — | no CVE | FoxIO lists IIS, Envoy, ngtcp2/nghttp3, and Google's quiche as not affected, each because it caps the unpacked headers while decoding rather than after. The amplification varies by stack, in FoxIO's own tests against default settings. On quic-go, a 1 MB compressed batch unpacked into about 160,000 header fields and left roughly 15 MB held in the request, about 17 times the bytes sent; quic-go's own advisory puts the possible expansion at around 50 times. A second method drives the ratio much higher: the attacker stores one roughly 4 KB header entry, then points at it thousands of times using one-byte references, and the server rebuilds the full entry on each reference. FoxIO measured about 4,000 times on Bun and between 600 and 1,800 times on lsquic. Bun carries a worst-case. Its HTTP/3 server, which Bun's documentation calls experimental, uses lsquic but replaces the part that caps header memory with its own code, which checks each header but never the running total. FoxIO found that once the unpacked headers pass 2 GB, a size counter in that code overflows to zero and the server enters a loop it never leaves. A single stream carrying about 516 KB on the wire, FoxIO reported, leaves the server stuck at 100 percent CPU with no recovery, blocking new requests. The missing running total is what lets the overflow be reached; lsquic's own 64 KB cap prevents it. Wireshark is a different case from the server flaws. Its issue crashes the HTTP/3 dissector, the part that reads HTTP/3 out of a capture, when Wireshark decrypts traffic using a key-log file or opens a capture file that holds decryption secrets. It is not a server an attacker reaches over the network. Wireshark said it is "unaware of any exploits for this issue." Operators should upgrade to the fixed releases above. For the stacks with no fix, FoxIO gives interim steps: on Bun, do not expose an HTTP/3 server; on mitmproxy, turn off HTTP/3 by passing --set http3=false; and for the h3 Rust library, set a sensible limit with max_field_section_size. The lsquic fix, released July 16, 2026, caps how many unpacked header sets a server holds per stream, defaulting to one. FoxIO said the work began after Gal Bar Nahum's research into "MadeYouReset," a denial-of-service technique against HTTP/2, which asked whether HTTP/3's header compression had a similar weakness.

6815f2a0b4a0d8cf: GitLab released fixes on October 21 for a flaw that lets an attacker run code on a self-managed server without logging in, and it affects every version of the software going back to 7.0, released in 2014. e2527452350fa74e: Google on Tuesday said it's rolling out improved safeguards in its Chrome browser to secure users against ClickFix attacks when Enhanced Protection is enabled. As part of these attacks, unsuspecting users who land on legitimate-but-compromised sites or click on malicious ads are redirected to phishing landing pages that display fake Cloudflare or Google reCAPTCHA verification or other non-existent errors and instruct users to copy and paste a command on the Windows Run dialog (or the Mac Terminal app) to address it. The moment a user presses the Enter key after pasting the command, it triggers a multi-stage infection chain that leads to the deployment of malware, such as information stealers or remote access trojans. In an attempt to blend in with regular activity and evade detection, the commands often make use of living-off-the-land (LotL) tools like PowerShell or cmd.exe to download next-stage payloads. A key reason why ClickFix remains an effective initial access method is that it flips the script on traditional phishing. Instead of exploiting sophisticated vulnerabilities or getting a user to click on suspicious links, it tricks them into opening the front door themselves under the pretext of troubleshooting a commonplace issue. "By shifting the download process out of the browser and into the terminal, attackers completely sidestep existing Chrome and Safe Browsing download protections," Google said. "To combat this technique, Chrome now detects when an Enhanced Protection user is tricked into copying suspicious commands." If a user copies a potential ClickFix script, the clipboard payload is scrubbed of any personal information it may contain and sent to Safe Browsing for further analysis. If the security system determines the command is dangerous, Chrome displays a warning. By doing so, the idea is to prevent the attack from taking place before the user executes the malicious command. Separately, Google is also introducing the following defenses in Chrome to tackle web scams for users who enable Enhanced Protection - - Establishing a taxonomy for Safe Browsing site warnings: Suspicious sites, which exhibit deceptive patterns commonly associated with known malicious sites, and Dangerous sites, which refer to sites that are known to be malicious and have a high risk of user harm. - Building upon on-device large language model (LLM)-based approaches to flag tech support scams and others, such as fake antivirus and browser update scams. "This model evaluates page content to analyze key indicators, such as the brand represented, the intent of the page, and a scam likeliness score, giving us rich threat data needed to identify deceptive sites," Google said. "Throughout this process, Chrome minimizes the amount of data shared with the server by only analyzing page text when a site exhibits high-confidence scam indicators. And whenever page content is sent off the device, it is processed ephemerally – meaning it is never logged, retained or used to train models." On Tuesday, Google said it's also introducing Financial Services Verification in the U.S. and Canada to validate an advertiser's credentials and ensure ads come from authorized financial providers.
