"Under this policy, advertisers must demonstrate they are authorized by relevant regulators or recognized registries before running certain financial ads – helping prevent brand impersonation and stopping bad actors from reaching people," Google said. "Alongside our ongoing work with financial regulators, we're working in the U.S. with the American Bankers Association to use their dedicated registry to verify authorized banks before ads can run. In Canada, we’re engaging closely with the Canadian Bankers Association as we prepare for our rollout." Apple Blocks Identity Resolution in Safari and WebKit The development comes as Apple revealed new privacy protections built into Safari and WebKit that block a practice called identity resolution, which turns email addresses into persistent tracking identifiers. The anti-tracking feature is available as part of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS 27 releases. "In this scheme, third parties (i.e., not the website owner) invisibly collect your email address when you log in or sign up for a newsletter," Apple's WebKit team said. "They send the email address to their servers, create an opaque tracking ID permanently linked to your email address, and send that tracking ID back to the web page." "The tracking ID is stored on the website and can from thereon be used for arbitrary purposes linked to your email address, such as building a profile of your browsing or targeting ads at you across websites. Logging out or unsubscribing from that newsletter does not remove the tracking ID or your email address stored with the third party." Apple said the third parties can build more data about users as they log in with their email address or fill in forms containing personal data, allowing them to create an identity graph with their name, residential address, phone number, and IP address. To prevent this sort of cross-site tracking, Safari blocks network access to identity resolution infrastructure embedded within the web pages, effectively stopping the third party from sending the email address to their servers. The blocking, Apple said, is done at the domain level. "It's not enough to block cross-site cookies to prevent cross-site tracking today because the tracking industry has not stopped trying to track users on the web," Apple said. 5ff1dd07c5c834bc: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a previously undocumented China-aligned threat cluster known as Bronze Sandcastle that has been observed targeting organizations in Asia and Africa since mid-2025. DLL sideloading is a popular adversarial technique that exploits the way Windows loads DLL files, allowing an attacker to trick a legitimate program into loading a malicious DLL. When an application is launched, it needs to load various DLLs in order to function correctly. If the application does not provide the full path to a required DLL, the operating system looks for it in a predetermined sequence of directories. An attacker can take advantage of this behavior by planting a malicious DLL with the same name as a legitimate one in a location that Windows searches before the folder that contains the actual DLL. "The threat group predominantly uses encrypted payload and configuration files that are decoded at runtime, meaning that static file-based detections may be ineffective," Sophos said. 2b1381b5788ddde4: Generative AI has changed what a malicious email looks like. Messages that once gave themselves away through clumsy wording, generic pretexts, and reused templates now arrive fluent, personalized, and unique to each recipient, and the behavioral signals email filters have relied on for years are fading as a result. Proofpoint shared several examples of the shift at its Protect 2026 conference. In one, a single threat actor contacted more than 30 real estate agents at the same company, each from a different account, about a different property, and in different words, before closing every thread with the same request: join a video meeting. Federal data points the same way. The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center counted more than 22,000 complaints involving AI in 2025, with nearly $900 million in associated losses, and logged 24,768 business email compromise (BEC) complaints with about $3.05 billion in reported losses, according to its 2025 Internet Crime Report. What AI Changed Email filters were built for attackers who had to cut corners. Researching a target, writing convincingly in a second language, impersonating a supplier, and producing enough variants to defeat signatures all took time, so attackers reused templates and infrastructure, and that reuse left patterns. Behavioral detection learned to spot them: new infrastructure, awkward language, odd timing, and requests that did not fit the conversation. Generative AI removes those constraints: - Language. Fluent, localized text in any language, with no typos or translation artifacts. - Context. Replies that fit the thread, the recipient’s role, and the timing. - Persona. Matched writing style, signature blocks, and fully fabricated conversation histories. - Variation. A unique message for every recipient, generated in seconds, so there is no template to match. The result, Proofpoint argues, is that behavior has become a weakening signal. When AI lets attackers make every message look normal, the analysis has to change too, from asking whether a message looks unusual to asking what it is trying to do. Thirty Conversations, One Ask The real estate campaign shows what that looks like in practice. Writing 30-plus distinct, plausible property enquiries, each tailored to a different listing and a different agent, is exactly the kind of work generative AI now does in seconds. The opening questions were mundane: whether a property was still open for inspection, what the price guide was, whether a viewing was possible that week. The sender mailboxes were real, and replies landed in threads the agents were already answering. | Figure 1. Different properties, senders, and wording, with the same final ask in every thread. | In one thread, an inspection enquiry sent at 2:58 a.m. turned into a meeting invitation 13 minutes later, complete with a branded template and a claim that the meeting required the agent’s “immediate attention.” The join link was a genuine google.com redirect, so reputation checks read clean, while a parameter in the URL handed the click to an unrelated site. Because each sender was making first contact, behavioral filters had no history to compare against, and because every message was different, there was no repeated content to match. What the messages shared was not how they looked but what they were trying to get the recipient to do. AI makes it easy to run this pattern against any business that depends on hearing from strangers, including clinics taking new patients, firms signing new clients, banks opening accounts, and insurers quoting policies, Proofpoint said. A variant aimed at insurance agents used quote requests, neighbor referrals, and coverage questions to build trust before sending a spoofed conference invitation that delivered the payload. AI-Powered Disruption AI has also made it easier to run campaigns that aim to disrupt rather than steal. Proofpoint described hostile communications campaigns in which hundreds or thousands of senders write to the same executives, each on a topic tailored to the target’s industry. Some messages carry derogatory language; others carry AI-generated or manipulated images that mock the recipient. | Figure 2. Hostile communications campaigns carry no payload. The signal is the pattern. | These messages have no link to detonate and no credential to harvest, and any one of them could pass for a single angry correspondent. Scoring messages one at a time will not catch them. The analysis has to recognize disruptive intent across the whole set, and read text and imagery together, since the hostility may sit in an AI-generated picture. Legitimacy on Demand The same shift applies to phishing infrastructure. One phishing-as-a-service kit Proofpoint highlighted presents a single flow behind four different disguises: a court access portal, a document-signing request, an identity check, and a finance report library. Each page displays a verification code and directs the victim to a legitimate sign-in page to paste it. Because the attacker generated the code, entering it authorizes the attacker’s session, a technique known as device-code phishing. | Figure 3. Four pretexts in front of one device-code flow. | Swapping the disguise is trivial for the operator, so the visual and linguistic fingerprints defenders might match change from one campaign to the next while the objective stays fixed. BEC shows AI’s effect on context most clearly. In another example, a single email contains a quoted thread in which an impersonated audit vendor and an executive at the target appear to agree on an invoice, a 50 percent loyalty rebate, and a payment date. The attached invoice itemizes audit phases, hours, and rates, and the closing line asks for payment that day to a remittance address that differs from the actual sending address. | Figure 4. A language model drafts all of it in seconds, which removes the effort that used to limit how many targets received this kind of attention. 9d349a6e395496ea: An AppSec team can point an AI agent running on a general-purpose model at its own web apps with little setup. Sure, the model writes the attacks. But everything that makes those attacks safe to run against production and worth acting on afterward lives in the harness around the model. The harness is where the engineering in AI pentesting sits. The Hugging Face intrusion OpenAI disclosed in July showed what happens when that harness gives way, even inside an OpenAI evaluation built to contain the agents. Why Each Control Takes Rigorous Engineering Let’s take a closer look at the attack different stages and the role AI agents can take there Scope A pentesting agent makes thousands of decisions about where to send its next request, and the model judges each one against a rule written in plain language. A web app’s real boundary often extends past one domain through redirects and calls to outside services. Enforcing scope means code that inspects every request before it leaves, and OWASP’s 2026 guidance routes privileged actions through a deterministic policy engine that checks them at execution time, outside the model. Credentials Finding exposed credentials is part of what a pentest does, so the agent regularly comes across working keys outside its assignment. Which of those it may use, for what, and when a person gets involved are policy decisions that the code around the model applies on every attempt. Prompt Injection Every page and API response the agent reads, including hidden fields, metadata and comments a user never sees, can carry content written by anyone who can post to the app. A single product review is enough to plant malicious instructions. OWASP ranks prompt injection the top risk for LLM applications and notes that no reliable prevention exists today. The design question is not whether the model gets fooled, but how much damage it can do if and when it does. That comes down to two things: how tightly each action is constrained and which actions require further inspection and human sign-off. Neither is simple. OWASP warns that approval fatigue degrades reviewer judgement at scale, so routing everything to a human simply shifts the failure point down the line. Proof In October 2026, Google stopped accepting product vulnerability reports to its open-source bug bounty program after a surge in automated submissions, the majority of which it said were not valid. A finding a developer can’t reproduce is just another ticket to close. Producing one worth acting on means running the exploit, capturing what it reached, and packaging the result so anyone can replay it, all within the limits of the other controls set. None of this is built once. Every model upgrade can change how the agent behaves, and every release changes the app whose security it tests. And around the controls sit the systems a production agent depends on, including change-triggered testing, routing findings to the developers who own the code, strictly controlling what customer data reaches a model provider, and connecting what the agent finds in the app to the rest of the environment. Across all of it, the pattern is the same. The model reasons about what to try, and deterministic code decides what runs, records it, and stops it when needed. How Pentera Apps Implements the Harness This separation of reasoning and execution is how we approach building Pentera Apps. Instead of letting an AI model send requests directly into an application, Pentera Apps pairs an AI that decides what to test with a deterministic harness that controls what runs. Every action is logged and any test can be paused or stopped at any time. It's the same safety discipline Pentera has applied to production testing for nearly a decade, across thousands of global customers. The harness also produces the proof. Every finding ships with a replayable exploit script, a CVSS 3.1 score and CWE mapping, so developers can reproduce the attack themselves instead of taking it on trust. Once the fix lands, the exact same attack can be re-run to confirm the path is closed. Tests run on demand or on a schedule, with change-triggered testing in CI/CD coming next, so validation stays inline with development. The surrounding systems follow the same discipline. Only minimal, redacted data reaches the LLM, with zero retention and no training on customer data, and data stays in the customer’s region. Every test starts with context from reconnaissance across the customer’s attack surfaces, findings from their security stack, and live threat intelligence signals. That context lets Pentera trace an exploit in a web app be traced into network, cloud, and identity on one platform. In agentic pentesting, the harness determines the results. Pentera Apps builds it in, so security teams get validated findings without building one themselves. Note: This article has been expertly written and contributed by Assaf Regev, AVP Product Marketing at Pentera. Security teams can sign up for early access to Pentera Apps, Agentic Web App Pentesting.
bf7cf33fc0ebbbd5: Attackers took control of more than 300 Tor exit relays in early October and used them to redirect SSH connections to servers that stole login passwords, a researcher found. Exit relays are the last hop in a Tor circuit, where traffic leaves the network for its destination. Only a password login to an SSH server made through Tor between October 1 and 5, after accepting the interception server's host key, could have been captured. The Tor Project began flagging relays on October 4, and by October 5, none remained in the consensus, the list of relays that Tor clients use. At the peak on October 4, the relays carrying the attacker's exit policy made up 7.46% of Tor's exit capacity, measured by consensus weight, according to an analysis of public Tor directory data posted to the tor-relays mailing list. The researcher, who publishes as kaba, scanned all of Tor's roughly 3,000 exits on October 2 and found 333 redirecting SSH to the same 12 interception servers. The directory-data analysis counts 377 relays run by 59 operators that switched to the attacker's exit policy between October 1 and 4, which it calls "a policy match, not proof of compromise." How the Hijacked Exits Intercepted SSH An exit relay only carries traffic to the ports its exit policy allows. The attackers rewrote that policy in the relays' torrc configuration files to allow port 22 (the SSH port), enabling SSH on 342 relays that had blocked it. Another 24 relays that had not been exits at all became exits. "It seems the attacker is gaining access to Linux based hosts and when these machines are running non-exits they are editing the torrc file and turning them into exits to be able to carry out the SSH attack," the Tor Project's network health team wrote in its October 5 notice to relay operators. Most of the affected relays were already exits, the directory data shows. The same change closed the encrypted mail ports, IMAPS and POP3S, and on most relays opened the plaintext-capable ones, POP3 and IMAP. A Tor client only picks an exit that allows the destination port, so these relays stopped carrying encrypted mail and started carrying SSH, Telnet, and, on most of them, plaintext mail. Why the encrypted mail ports were closed is not visible in the data, the analysis says. With port 22 open, an SSH connection through one of these exits went to one of 12 interception servers instead of its destination, kaba found. When a server intercepted the connection, it presented its own host key. A user who already knew the real server's key saw OpenSSH's warning that the remote host identification had changed, and a user connecting for the first time saw the usual prompt to accept a new key. In the October 2 scan, about a dozen exits were serving a fake host key, and the other 300 or so redirected through the same servers without altering the key. A user who accepted the key and typed a password handed it to the interceptor. The interceptor connected to the real server, so the session worked, and every command could be watched and separately logged in with the stolen password to check for sudo and run a base64-encoded Perl installer. In kaba's honeypot, the installer took the same form as the command that put Ebury, a backdoor that hides inside OpenSSH, on one of a relay operator's servers, as described below. A key-based SSH login could not be relayed this way. Under the SSH authentication protocol, , the client's signature includes an identifier unique to each session, so a signature made for the interceptor's session is useless against the real server. The interceptor could still accept a key login itself and show a fake shell, but it could not reach the real server with it. A password, by contrast, travels inside the encrypted session and can be read by the server at the other end, which here was the interceptor. Who Was Exposed, and What to Do If You Were To be exposed, someone had to connect to an SSH server over Tor between October 1 and the afternoon of October 5, land on one of the hijacked exits, have the connection intercepted rather than passed through, accept the interceptor's host key, and log in with a password. No count of victims exists. If you accepted an unfamiliar or changed host key over Tor in that window, treat the password you typed as stolen, change it, and check that server for the Ebury signs listed below. An OpenSSH client that accepted the key saved it in known_hosts. The server that intercepted kaba's connection used an ED25519 key with the fingerprint SHA256:6baCZCPsl+AfQuujUS81fMEE/C7UeJ+AwjrImqmDB3E, though the other interception servers may have used different keys. How It Was Found and Stopped Kaba encountered the attack on the morning of October 2, when an SSH connection over Tor returned a changed-key warning. He then used exitmap, a scanning tool that the Tor Project's network health team also uses, to open an SSH connection from one of his servers to another via each exit in turn. One end checked whether the host key was correct, and the other whether the connection originated at the exit or from an interception server. He reported the results to the health team that evening. The health team also spotted the policy change through its own monitoring. On October 4, it contacted Zimmer, who ran the Quetzalcoatl relay family, the largest group of affected relays, and Zimmer confirmed the change was not his, asked for the relays to be marked bad, and stopped Tor on the server running them. Directory authorities began voting the BadExit and MiddleOnly flags on affected relays at 18:00 UTC that day, and the flags were in the consensus by 21:00. BadExit tells Tor clients never to use a relay as an exit. On the morning of October 5,, a scripted restart swept through 55 of Quetzalcoatl's hosts, with the policy still in place.
cb2237817d8d4ca2: Unknown hackers hijacked more than 300 Tor exit nodes and reconfigured them to favor unencrypted email traffic and redirect SSH connections through servers they controlled, a researcher reported Tuesday. The hijacking began in late August, when, according to Tor volunteers, the attacker used a valid password that had been reused to gain access to a Tor management server. The attacker then installed Ebury, a backdoor written for Linux that was discovered 12 years ago. Mysteries remain Then the attacker connected from the management server to a second Tor server, called Switzerland2, through SSH, using an RSA key that, for unknown reasons, investigators couldn’t find among Switzerland2’s authorized keys. With administrative control of Switzerland2, the attackers installed Ebury there as well. Finally, the attacker reconfigured settings on two exit nodes that Switzerland2 hosted. Ultimately, 333 exit relays were involved in the SSH and email interception campaign, although investigators haven’t established how the attackers gained control of all the underlying servers. The attackers then reconfigured the servers. One set of changes redirected SSH traffic traversing Tor to one of 12 attacker-controlled interceptor servers. Tor users who ignored warnings that the SSH host key had changed would then enter their SSH passwords. A second set of changes caused the exit nodes to block ports 25, 465, 587, 993, and 995—used to accept various forms of encrypted email—while continuing to allow ports for receiving unencrypted email. If email services downgraded the connections, the attackers used their access to the exit nodes to obtain unencrypted messages. It’s unclear whether any such downgrade attempts succeeded. Tuesday’s report revealed many new details, including how many exit nodes were compromised and how the attackers used them to redirect SSH traffic. “If you happen to get a circuit that exits over one of those 333 infected exit nodes, you won’t notice anything at first,” Kaba, the name of the Tor volunteer who authored the post, wrote. “Encrypted web traffic is forwarded as usual, but if you attempt an SSH connection over Port 22, you’re unknowingly redirected to one of 12 SSH interception servers. f0182a53b406878e: Unknown threat actors breached TeamUpdraft's website and potentially gained unauthorized access to customers' connection keys for UpdraftCentral, UpdraftVault, and UpdraftClone, using them to backdoor WordPress sites. TeamUpdraft is the developer behind UpdraftPlus, a popular WordPress backup plugin with over four million active installations. The vendor also offers UpdraftCentral, a remote management service that's used for managing multiple sites remotely. A client component of UpdraftCentral is shipped within every copy of UpdraftPlus. "Over the weekend of 17-18 October we identified unauthorized access to the teamupdraft.com website," TeamUpdraft said in a statement. "Our team responded straight away and worked through the night to contain it – we closed the access route, signed out every account and replaced the keys and credentials that could have been affected." As a result of the incident, threat actors are believed to have accessed its customer database, which holds the following information - - Names, email addresses, billing addresses and order history - Account passwords, stored only in hashed (scrambled) form and never in plain text - Two-factor authentication (2FA) settings - Connection keys for UpdraftCentral, UpdraftVault and UpdraftClone TeamUpdraft said the database does not hold any financial information, and that they are handled by Stripe and PayPal. It also emphasized that the UpdraftPlus plugin, along with self-hosted versions of UpdraftCentral and backups sent to customers' own remote storage, are not impacted. "However, if your site was accessed through UpdraftCentral, please also re-authorise your remote storage and change any storage access keys, as a precaution," it said. In addition, TeamUpdraft said it deployed a fix to address the underlying issue, signed out every teamupdraft.com account and reset login security across the site, and released UpdraftPlus 1.26.13 (free) and 2.26.13 (Premium) to automatically disconnect every UpdraftCentral connection made before 10 p.m. BST on October 18, 2026, to prevent the old keys from working. Other steps taken by the developer are listed below - - Disconnected every site from UpdraftVault and issued new credentials - Replaced every UpdraftClone client key - Rotated its keys with payment providers and other connected services - Implemented additional monitoring in place - Reported the incident to the U.K. Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) and other relevant authorities Users who have a teamupdraft.com account are advised to change their password with immediate effect (and elsewhere, if the same password has been reused), reset 2FA settings, and exercise caution when receiving unexpected emails claiming to be from TeamUpdraft. TeamUpdraft is also recommending that cloud customers of UpdraftCentral follow the steps below as soon as possible, since the connection keys can send commands to the connected sites - - Log in to the site's own WordPress dashboard, not through UpdraftCentral. - Update UpdraftPlus to version 1.26.12 (free) or 2.26.12 (Premium) or later. - Disconnect it from UpdraftCentral: go to Settings > UpdraftPlus > Advanced Tools > UpdraftCentral and delete the connection key. - Go to Users and check for any administrator accounts you don’t recognise. Remove them. - Go to Plugins, including the Must-Use tab if you can see it, and check for anything you don’t recognise. Remove it. - Change the passwords for all administrator accounts on the site. - If you find anything suspicious, consider restoring the site from a backup taken before 17 October. - Reconnect the site to UpdraftCentral. UpdraftVault users are being urged to reconnect their sites to the backup service, and UpdraftClone users who have created a client key are required to copy the new keys from My Account > UpdraftClone > UpdraftClone Key Management and share them with their clients. The development comes as WordPress security company Patchstack said it observed an attacker holding valid UpdraftCentral dashboard keys issuing commands to install backdoor plugins on connected WordPress sites. The campaign is said to have run continuously through an 18-hour window on October 18 and 19, 2026. "The attacker sends a signed plugin.upload_plugin command over the plugin's remote procedure call channel, which listens on ordinary POST requests to the site root. WordPress installs and activates the supplied plugin through its standard installer," Patchstack security researcher Dave Jong said. Slovakia-based penetration testing company Nethemba, which first detected the attack in the wild, has described the rogue plugin as a backdoor that hooks into every request to the site to check if the URL contains the parameter "?_9f5696=" and compares it with a 32-character token. If a matching token is detected, it creates a user "data-ops43" with the display name "Site Tools," assigns it the Editor role, and grants the account "manage_options" and "install_plugins" permissions, allowing the operator to upload arbitrary PHP plugins and open site settings. "Enabling registration and setting the default role to administrator is enough for the attacker to create a full administrator," Nethemba said. "On a standard WordPress site, an Editor also has unfiltered_html, so the account can put JavaScript into posts that runs in the browser of every administrator." "The backdoor has a second layer as well. The account it creates, with a known password, stays in WordPress even after the plugin is removed, and the attacker can log in with it through the normal login form unless two-factor authentication is enabled for that account." 503b4db3bf44591c: U.S. federal civilian agencies must remove DeepSeek products from their information technology systems, along with any third-party products or services "developed using DeepSeek implementations," under a Department of Homeland Security order. They may also no longer buy information technology products or services from the Chinese AI developer or its affiliates Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin issued the order, dated July 24, 2026, under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018, and the department published it in the Federal Register on October 20. The notice does not define "DeepSeek implementations." The order names Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co., Ltd., the developer of the R1 and V3 models, and covers its affiliates as defined in federal acquisition rules. The company's privacy policy says it collects, processes and stores users' personal data in the People's Republic of China. Under the 2018 law, the Federal Acquisition Security Council recommends exclusion and removal orders, and three officials may issue them: the Secretary of Homeland Security for civilian agencies, the Secretary of Defense for the Defense Department and national security systems, and the Director of National Intelligence for the intelligence community. The DeepSeek order therefore covers only what civilian agencies buy and run. It does not restrict companies or the public. The 2018 law was first used in 2025, when the Director of National Intelligence excluded Acronis, a Swiss cybersecurity and data protection company, from intelligence community procurement and ordered its products removed from intelligence community systems. Executive agencies "shall comply with exclusion and removal orders," the law says. An agency can ask the official who issued an order for an exception, and under the council's regulations the request must be in writing and give a compelling justification. DHS directs questions about the order to CISA's FASCSA Order Implementation Team at fascsa.orders@cisa.dhs.gov. The order also reaches government contractors. A federal contract that carries FAR clause 52.204-30 bars the contractor from providing or using, in performing the contract, any product or service covered by an applicable FASCSA order, unless the issuing official has granted a waiver. The clause also requires the contractor to: - Search SAM.gov for the phrase "FASCSA order" at least once every three months - Make a reasonable inquiry into its supply chain when a new order could affect it - Report any covered product or service it has provided or used to the contracting officer within 3 business days of identifying it - Send further information on mitigation within 10 business days of that report - Include the clause in its subcontracts An order issued after a solicitation applies to an existing contract only once the contracting officer adds it by amendment or modification. The Federal Register notice gives no reasons for the order. The signed order is attached to the notice as four scanned pages and is posted on regulations.gov under docket DHS-2026-0628. The order is dated July 24. DHS filed it for public inspection at the Federal Register on October 19, 87 days later, and it was published the next day. The council's regulations leave public release of an order to the issuing official, who "May provide a copy of the order to other persons, including through public disclosure." They set no deadline for it. The law requires the issuing official to notify the company named in an order and the appropriate congressional committees, and to review the order at least once a year. Before the order, U.S. restrictions on DeepSeek were device bans adopted one body at a time. By February 2025, Congress, NASA, the Navy, the Pentagon and Texas had barred DeepSeek from government devices. Bills to bar DeepSeek on government devices were introduced in the House and Senate that month and had not advanced past committee as of October 21. China's foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said at a briefing on October 20 that "China consistently opposes the overstretching of the concept of national security" and that Beijing will "resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies," the Associated Press reported. DeepSeek did not immediately respond to the AP's request for comment.
2f30cd1c0af42cce: State Bank of India has identified 3,897 customer records containing personal information in a set of about 375,000 records available on the dark web, and it does not yet know where the data came from. The state-owned bank, India's largest, said in a stock-exchange filing dated October 21 that it "has experienced an incident involving the loss of certain data." The count is preliminary, and the bank has yet to establish whether the data is authentic, how far the exposure goes and what risk it poses to customers. The exposed information "reportedly included customers' registered mobile numbers, dates of birth, names, gender, email addresses, residential addresses, branch and CIF identifiers, lead IDs, and metadata associated with loan/lead records and other related files," in the filing's words. A CIF identifier is the customer information file number, the bank's internal ID for each customer. The bank has not said whether the 3,897 records belong to 3,897 different people, or what the rest of the set contains. The 3,897 are roughly 1 in 100 of the records it examined. Account numbers, balances, passwords, one-time passcodes, card details and government identity numbers such as PAN or Aadhaar are not among the categories the filing lists. The risk in the listed categories is impersonation: a caller or message that uses a customer's name, mobile number, date of birth, address, branch, and internal ID to appear to come from the bank. The alert reached the bank on October 16 via its threat intelligence provider, CERT-In, India's national computer emergency response team, and the Defense Cyber Agency, the armed forces' cyber agency under the Ministry of Defense. The bank activated its incident response and containment procedures and engaged an independent cybersecurity firm from CERT-In's panel of approved security auditors to assess what the filing calls "the alleged compromise." The incident has no material impact on the bank's core business operations, financial performance or business continuity, the filing says. That covers the bank's business, not its customers. The filing names no attacker, forum or dataset. The figure of about 375,000 matches a claim that the monitoring account CyberPulse56 flagged on X on October 16. The account said a threat actor using the name Siriusim claimed to have leaked customer documents and personal data linked to SBI: 375,000 rows in CSV format and 2,722 PDF documents, said to include personal information, loan applications and supporting documents, account-opening forms and addresses. The Free Press Journal examined the listing on BreachForums, a cybercrime forum used to trade stolen data, and found 4 sample records posted with the listing. The phone numbers in the samples were valid. The WhatsApp profile picture on one number matched the passport-size photograph on that person's KYC document, which the actor had also posted. That check covers 4 records and does not show that the whole set is genuine or where it came from. The samples were mostly loan-related and carried KYC fields, and they did not show whether the data belonged to SBI itself, one of its subsidiaries, or a third-party provider that handles banking applications. Nothing in the bank's filing ties its analysis to the listing, and the bank has not said whether the 2,722 PDF documents were part of what it examined. Whether any SBI system was breached is an open question. The filing leaves the source of the data to the investigation and gives no date for when the data first appeared. The filing does not mention whether affected customers have been or will be told. The bank's cyber security page, last updated in June, tells customers to report any cyber incident to report.phishing@sbi.co.in or the national cybercrime helpline, 1930. That is general advice, written before the incident. Bank of Baroda, another state-owned bank, told the exchanges on July 27 about a cyber-security incident in nearly the same words, including "the alleged compromise," after receiving "a communication from an anonymous source claiming access to certain data." That filing named a preliminary cause, "potential business email compromise." SBI's names none.
37c3e5fa7177b271: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday added four vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, including four vulnerabilities impacting Plex Media Server that's collectively called Plex2Shell. The vulnerabilities are listed below - - CVE-2026-96652 (CVSS score: 5.3) - Plex Media Server Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability - CVE-2026-96654 (CVSS score: 6.9) - Plex Media Server improper neutralization of encoded URI schemes in a web page Vulnerability - CVE-2026-96655 (CVSS score: 5.3) - Plex Media Server Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability - CVE-2026-96656 (CVSS score: 8.6) - Plex Media Server external control of file name or path Vulnerability According to security researcher Zach Main, who discovered and reported the vulnerabilities, a remote attacker could chain the four vulnerabilities to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution. The issues were addressed in Plex Media Server 1.43.3.10861 released on August 3, 2026. The addition of the four vulnerabilities to the KEV catalog follows a report from security researcher boredhackerblog, who found that threat actors are weaponizing the flaws to deploy cryptocurrency miners and proxy malware. CISA has also flagged two other vulnerabilities as actively exploited. One of them is a DLL sideloading vulnerability in Siemens Software Center (CVE-2026-110936, CVSS score: 8.4) that has been abused in ClickFix attacks using a platform called Romulus. The second security flaw is a command injection bug in EG Secure Solutions SiteGuard Server Edition (CVE-2026-106931, CVSS score: 8.5) that the Japanese company confirmed as being exploited. No additional details related to the exploitation activity are currently available. CISA is urging Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies to apply fixes for CVE-2026-106931, CVE-2026-96656, and CVE-2026-96654 by October 23, 2026, and the rest by November 3, 2026.
8dbb0ccea4784e45: A Belarus-aligned hacktivist group spent nearly two years within the network of a Russian healthcare organization. According to a report published by Russian cybersecurity firm Solar, the activity has been attributed to a threat cluster dubbed Partisan Zmiy, which is also known as the Cyber Partisans. Known to be active since at least 2020, the group has a track record of striking industrial enterprises and government agencies in Russia and Belarus with a backdoor called Vasilek that uses Telegram for command-and-control (C2) and data exfiltration. Some of the attacks have also leveraged phishing lures to deliver an installer that simultaneously deploys the legitimate FortiClient VPN program on the system as well as an open-source program known as DNSCat2 that allows attackers to gain control of the infected host. A notable aspect of the threat actor is their ability to stage destructive attacks with a wiper referred to as Pryanik, alongside taking steps to systematically clear Windows event logs using a utility dubbed Evlx. The Rostelecom subsidiary said it discovered the intrusion in December 2025, although evidence suggests that the earliest signs of compromise date back to early 2024. The name of the targeted organization was not identified. The exact initial access vector used to breach the entity is also not known. Unlike other attacks linked to Cyber Partisans, the threat actors remained on the network for an extended period of time without carrying out any destructive activity, marking something of a shift in modus operandi. "The attacked organization possessed an extensive infrastructure and two-way trusted relationships with numerous subsidiary medical institutions," Solar said. "We hypothesize that the lack of infrastructure disruption is due precisely to the value of this access for further espionage and trusted relationship attacks." Observed as part of the intrusion is a loader-scheduler service ("vmauad") that masquerades as a legitimate VMware component to maintain persistence and evade cursory inspection. To accomplish this, the attackers are said to have taken advantage of a trusted-but-unmonitored VMware Tools directory location to plant malicious executables or replace legitimate VMware DLLs with a malicious version ("vmtools.dll") containing the backdoor. The primary responsibility of the Windows service is to launch the rogue binary "C:\Program Files\VMware\VMware Tools\authd.exe" that, besides launching a GOST tunnel every Saturday from 10 p.m. to 11 p.m., runs an updated version of Vasilek (version 1.5.8) once, eight hours after the service begins. Once installed, Vasilek is equipped to collect information about an infected computer, execute Windows commands, launch and terminate processes, transfer files, capture screenshots, record keystrokes, and escalate privileges via runas. It can also prevent the machine from going into sleep mode, and update or remove itself. One new addition is the "move_cursor" command that, as the name implies, allows the backdoor to move the cursor and simulate user input on the victim's screen. "The group consistently invests in stealth and operational security, rather than new capabilities: hostname binding in two independent components, nightly scheduled payload launches, system proxy inheritance, disguise as legitimately installed but unused software, file rotation across the same paths, time-stomping, outgoing message suppression, and anonymous messages on behalf of the group in operator chats," Solar said. "The backdoor's feature set has remained largely unchanged over four revisions. Due to Telegram being blocked in Russia by ISPs, communication between the Vasilek backdoor and C2 has become unstable." The disclosure comes as Solar also disclosed details of a phishing campaign that employs JavaScript attachments mimicking business-themed documents, such as payments and purchase orders, to deliver a previously unreported malware family known as HypeAgent. The Windows malware is a full-featured trojan designed to take complete control over infected systems, packing the ability to steal files, open a console, change desktop wallpaper, turn on a webcam, log keystrokes, launch hidden VNC and RDP sessions, control the mouse, and even deploy a cryptocurrency miner. It's also capable of stealing cookies associated with Discord, Steam, GitHub, Instagram, Telegram, Binance, ChatGPT, Claude, and Cursor, and tampering with the installed Exodus wallet app to inject JavaScript that can collect the victim's password, PIN, mnemonic phrase, and private key. Earlier this June, Solar also observed legitimate infrastructure compromised by the ProxyCB proxyware botnet malware making automated requests to Russian websites and online platforms, while identifying possible overlaps between the botnet infrastructure and historical activity linked to TeamSpy, a threat cluster known for abusing TeamViewer to facilitate reconnaissance and data theft. Last month, the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) charged Searzhudin Tamirlanovich Aktulaev, a 40-year-old Russian national extradited from Cyprus in May 2025, for exploiting an online messaging service of a well-known freelance employment platform to send malware-laced Excel attachments to about 80,000 of its users in 2016 and 2017 using 255 fake accounts. The attacks led to the deployment of two types of malware, a variant of the TVRAT (aka Sheldor, SpyAgent, TeamBot, TeamSpy, and TVSPY) and DarkVNC, to harvest and send data from a victim computer to a remote server under the attacker's control. Thousands of computers are assessed to have been infected as a result of this scheme.
